title: Pulmonary Embolism
sub: Post-op day 2, hip replacement · Orthopedic unit
profile: 71-year-old woman, post-op day 2 after a right total hip replacement. History of atrial fibrillation and a stroke 3 years ago; her home warfarin was held 5 days before surgery.

Notes: Nurses' notes 10:15

Client called for help after walking to the bathroom with physical therapy. Reports sudden shortness of breath and a sharp right-sided chest pain that is worse when she takes a deep breath. Anxious, states "something is wrong." Diaphoretic. Breath sounds decreased at the right base. Right calf swollen, warm and tender to touch. Hip incision clean, dry and intact. Alert and oriented × 4.
Nurses' notes 07:00
Resting comfortably. Incisional pain 3/10 after oral analgesic. Bowel sounds active. Voided 300 mL clear yellow urine. Ambulated 20 feet with walker and PT.
Vitals: BP 128/76 mm Hg · HR 118 (irregular) · RR 28 · SpO₂ 88% on room air · T 37.9 °C (100.2 °F)
BP 132/78 · HR 84 (irregular) · RR 16 · SpO₂ 96% on room air · T 37.1 °C
Labs: D-dimer elevated · Hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL · Hematocrit 33% · Platelets 230,000/mm³ · aPTT 30 seconds (baseline) · Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL
Orders: Oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥ 92% · Head of bed up · CT scan of the chest (pulmonary embolism protocol) · Venous Doppler, right leg · Heparin IV bolus and continuous infusion, weight-based, adjusted by aPTT per pharmacy protocol · Bleeding precautions

items.stem: Tap the findings in the 10:15 assessment that are consistent with a pulmonary embolism.
passage: Sharp chest pain worse with a deep breath
Hip incision clean, dry and intact
items.rationale: The book lists the usual PE findings as sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain (pain worse on breathing in), tachypnea, tachycardia and anxiety, plus leg swelling from the deep vein thrombosis that often sends the clot. A clean incision is a normal post-op finding. Being alert and having a normal blood pressure are reassuring: confusion and hypotension would point to a massive PE.

items.stem: For each item in the client's history, indicate whether the book classifies it as a strong or a moderate risk factor for venous thromboembolism (VTE).
rows: Right total hip replacement 2 days ago
items.rationale: Table 2 lists hip or knee replacement and recent major surgery as strong VTE risk factors. Atrial fibrillation and a history of stroke are moderate risk factors. This client has several at once, and her usual anticoagulant was stopped for surgery, so a clot in the leg traveling to the lung fits her picture.

items.stem: Complete the sentence.

blanks.pre: The client's findings are most consistent with
so the nurse must watch closely for

items.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia and a swollen calf point to a PE, not a wound problem. Her blood pressure is normal and she is fully alert, so this is a symptomatic PE rather than a massive one. Table 2.1 lists hypotension, cold mottled skin, confusion and decreased consciousness as signs of a massive PE, so those are the changes that would show she is getting worse.

items.stem: For each intervention, indicate whether it is anticipated or not anticipated for this client right now.
rows: IV heparin bolus and infusion adjusted by aPTT
Venous Doppler of the right leg
Discharge home today on an oral factor Xa inhibitor alone
items.rationale: The book's treatment for a symptomatic PE is hospital care with an IV heparin bolus plus infusion, dosed by weight and adjusted by aPTT. A CT scan helps confirm the PE, and a venous Doppler finds the source clot. Thrombolytics such as alteplase are for a massive PE with hypotension and low bleeding risk; this client is stable and only 2 days after surgery. An oral factor Xa inhibitor alone is the book's approach for an asymptomatic PE, which she does not have.

items.stem: The heparin infusion has been started. Which actions should the nurse include in the client's care? Select all that apply.
options: Check for nosebleeds, blood in the urine and new bruising
Cluster blood draws to limit venipunctures
Massage the right calf to relieve the swelling
Give the as-needed pain medicine by intramuscular injection
Encourage at least 2 L of fluid per day unless restricted
Keep the bed low and assist the client when she gets up
items.rationale: During anticoagulant therapy the book says to monitor for bleeding (epistaxis, hematuria, bruising, a drop in H/H), limit invasive procedures such as venipunctures and injections, and keep the environment safe for clients who walk. Hydration of at least 2 L a day is an independent nursing intervention if fluids are not restricted. IM injections are the kind of invasive procedure to avoid while anticoagulated, and rubbing a leg that holds a clot risks breaking off more of it.

items.stem: Twenty-four hours after heparin was started: for each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or needs follow-up.
rows: SpO₂ 95% on 2 L nasal cannula, RR 20
items.rationale: Better oxygenation, a slower heart rate and less pain show the PE is responding to treatment. Hematuria, new bruising and a drop in hemoglobin are the bleeding signs the book says to watch for during anticoagulation, so the nurse reports them and expects the aPTT and heparin rate to be reviewed.

title: Tension Pneumothorax
sub: Left rib fractures after a motorcycle crash · Trauma step-down unit
profile: 34-year-old man admitted 6 hours ago after a motorcycle crash with fractures of the left 4th to 6th ribs. No past medical history.

Notes: Nurses' notes 14:20

Client suddenly reports he "can't get air in." Severe dyspnea, sitting bolt upright and gripping the side rails. Trachea deviated to the right. Neck veins distended. Breath sounds absent on the left. Skin pale and cool. Pain at the left rib fractures 6/10. Bruising over the left lateral chest wall from the crash.
Nurses' notes 12:00
Breathing comfortably on 2 L nasal cannula. Trachea midline. Breath sounds slightly diminished at the left base. Rib pain 5/10, using incentive spirometer to 1,500 mL.
Vitals: BP 84/50 mm Hg · HR 132 (sinus tachycardia) · RR 36 · SpO₂ 82% on 2 L nasal cannula · T 37.2 °C (99 °F)
Labs: Hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL · WBC 10,800/mm³ · Glucose 112 mg/dL · Na⁺ 139 mEq/L · K⁺ 4.0 mEq/L
Chest x-ray: fractures of left ribs 4–6; small left pneumothorax
Orders: Oxygen 2 L nasal cannula, titrate to SpO₂ ≥ 92% · Continuous pulse oximetry · Incentive spirometer every hour while awake · Analgesic as prescribed for pain · Notify provider for respiratory distress or SBP < 90 mm Hg

items.stem: Which findings at 14:20 are signs of a tension pneumothorax? Select all that apply.
options: Bruising over the left chest wall
items.rationale: The book lists the signs of a tension pneumothorax as distended neck veins, hypotension, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, and tachycardia. All four are new since 12:00. Rib pain and chest-wall bruising are expected after the crash and were present before, and the temperature is normal.

items.stem: What best explains why the client's trachea is now pushed to the right?
options: Air trapped in the left pleural space is building pressure and pushing the chest structures toward the right
The right lung has collapsed and is pulling the trachea toward it
The fractured left ribs have shifted inward against the trachea
Pain is making the client turn his head and neck to the right
items.rationale: In a tension pneumothorax, trapped air builds pressure in the affected (left) pleural space and pushes the trachea away from the affected side. In a simple spontaneous or traumatic pneumothorax the book notes the trachea, if it moves at all, shifts toward the affected side. The right lung is not the injured side, and rib fractures or head position do not move the trachea.

items.stem: Complete the diagram: the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take now, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

opts: Call the rapid response team and stay with the client
Wait for a repeat chest x-ray before calling the provider
Have the client use the incentive spirometer and recheck in 30 minutes
Give the prescribed analgesic and reassess in an hour
Oxygen saturation and work of breathing

items.rationale: Tracheal deviation away from the injured side, distended neck veins, hypotension and tachycardia after chest trauma mean a tension pneumothorax, which the book calls life-threatening and a medical emergency. A stable small pneumothorax would not cause shock, and pain or pneumonia would not shift the trachea. The nurse calls for emergency help at once and stays with the client, and increases supplemental oxygen (the book's first measure for a large pneumothorax), rather than waiting for imaging or trying spirometry. By current practice the provider relieves the trapped air immediately with emergency needle (or finger) decompression, followed by a chest tube to re-establish negative pleural pressure; a chest tube alone is not the first step. Blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation and work of breathing show whether the pressure on the heart and lung is being relieved.

items.stem: The provider decompressed the left chest and then placed a left chest tube connected to a water-seal drainage system. For each nursing action, indicate whether it is appropriate or inappropriate.
rows: Keep the drainage collection chamber lower than the chest
Arrange the tubing so it has no dependent loops
Clamp the chest tube whenever the client walks in the hall
Give pain medicine as needed so he can breathe deeply
Rest the drainage system on the bed next to the client's chest
items.rationale: The book's chest tube rules: keep the collection chamber lower than the chest, avoid dependent loops in the tubing, and clamp only when changing the system with a physician order. Treating pain as needed is part of large-pneumothorax care. Clamping for walks can trap air again, and a drainage system level with the chest lets fluid flow back toward the client.

items.stem: On rounds the nurse finds the drainage system sitting on the bed at the level of the client's chest, with a long loop of tubing hanging below the mattress and holding fluid. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Place the drainage system upright below chest level and straighten the tubing so fluid can drain
Clamp the chest tube, then move the drainage system
Disconnect the tubing to empty the fluid in the loop into the chamber
Leave the system in place and document the findings
items.rationale: The chamber must stay lower than the chest, and dependent loops trap fluid and block drainage. Fixing both restores drainage. The book says to clamp only when changing the system with a physician order, disconnecting opens the system to air, and leaving it as is allows fluid to back up.

items.stem: The next morning: for each finding, indicate whether it shows that treatment is effective or that it needs follow-up.
rows: SpO₂ 96% on 2 L nasal cannula, breathing comfortably
Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber
Neck veins flat with the head of the bed at 45°
items.rationale: A midline trachea, flat neck veins, normal blood pressure and heart rate, and good oxygen saturation show that the trapped air has been removed and the lung is re-expanding. Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber signals an air leak (the book: bubbling in the water seal is a sign of an air leak), so the nurse checks the system from the dressing to the drainage unit and reports it. Note that brief, intermittent bubbling with exhaling or coughing can be expected while air is still leaving the pleural space after a pneumothorax; it is continuous bubbling that points to a leak.

title: Inferior STEMI with Right Ventricular Involvement
sub: Chest pain at home · Emergency department
profile: 61-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia brought in by ambulance with chest pressure. No known drug allergies, no bleeding history, no recent use of sildenafil or tadalafil.

Notes: ED triage 19:05

Crushing chest pressure that started 45 minutes ago while mowing the lawn and has not let up with rest. Pain 8/10, radiating to the jaw. Diaphoretic, short of breath, nauseated. Lungs clear in all fields. Neck veins distended at 45°. Ate dinner 2 hours ago. States his brother had a "heart stent" last year.
12-lead ECG 19:09
Sinus bradycardia, rate 56. ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Right-sided leads: ST elevation in V4R.
Vitals: BP 88/56 mm Hg · HR 56 · RR 22 · SpO₂ 95% on room air · T 36.8 °C (98.2 °F)
Labs: Troponin I elevated · Glucose 132 mg/dL · K⁺ 4.2 mEq/L · Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL · Hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL
Orders: Activate cardiac catheterization lab for primary PCI · Aspirin 324 mg chewable, non-enteric-coated, PO now · 0.9% sodium chloride IV bolus as prescribed · Atorvastatin 80 mg PO · Continuous cardiac monitoring

items.stem: Tap the findings that are hallmark signs of an ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI).
passage: ST elevation in II, III and aVF
items.rationale: The book's hallmark signs of STEMI are chest pain or symptoms lasting more than 20 minutes, diaphoresis and shortness of breath, with ST elevation on the ECG from a completely blocked coronary artery. A recent meal, a family history, a normal temperature and a mildly raised glucose do not identify a STEMI.

items.stem: Complete the sentence.

blanks.pre: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF shows an
in the area supplied by the
and ST elevation in V4R means the infarct also involves the

items.rationale: On the book's ECG map, leads II, III and aVF view the inferior wall, which the right coronary artery (RCA) supplies. Anterior MI shows in V1–V4 and involves the LAD; lateral MI shows in I, aVL, V5 and V6. Right-sided leads V3R–V4R detect a right ventricular infarct, which often comes with an inferior MI.

items.stem: Which explanation best accounts for the client's low blood pressure with clear lungs?
options: The infarcted right ventricle is pumping poorly, so preload to the left heart is already low
The left ventricle is failing and backing fluid into the lungs
A pericardial effusion is compressing the heart
items.rationale: With a right ventricular infarct (ST elevation in V4R), the book notes that preload is already low: the weak right ventricle cannot push enough blood through the lungs to the left heart, so blood backs up into the neck veins (distended at 45°) while the lungs stay clear and the blood pressure falls. Left-sided failure would cause crackles. He has nausea but has not been vomiting, and nothing in the record suggests a pericardial effusion. Recognizing low preload matters because it changes which MI drugs are safe.

items.stem: Which treatments are appropriate for this client before he goes to the cath lab? Select all that apply.
options: 0.9% sodium chloride IV bolus as prescribed
items.rationale: Aspirin 162–325 mg, chewed and non-enteric-coated, is given immediately. A right ventricular infarct is treated with IV fluids (and positive inotropes if needed), and a high-intensity statin is started as soon as possible. The book says to avoid nitrates and diuretics in a right ventricular infarct because they worsen an already low preload, and to avoid morphine in right ventricular MI for the same reason. Beta-blockers are started only when there is no bradycardia or hypotension; this client has both.

items.stem: After a successful PCI through the right femoral artery, the nurse removes the sheath. The client becomes pale and nauseated, HR 44, BP 78/46 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Keep direct pressure on the site and give the prescribed atropine and IV fluid bolus
Release pressure briefly to look for a hematoma, then raise the head of the bed
Start the prescribed nitroglycerin infusion because the artery may be closing again
Stop the IV fluids to prevent overload and recheck vital signs in 15 minutes
items.rationale: This is the vasovagal response the book warns about during sheath removal: hypotension with bradycardia. The book says to give atropine for bradycardia, give a fluid bolus, hold nitrates (preload reducers), manage pain and anxiety, and keep direct pressure on the site for at least 20 minutes. Releasing pressure risks bleeding from the femoral artery, nitroglycerin would drop the pressure further, and stopping fluids removes the volume he needs.

items.stem: Review the findings recorded after PCI. For each one, indicate whether it is an expected sign of reperfusion or a complication the nurse must report now.
rows: Sudden rise in troponin right after the artery is opened
New back and flank pain with falling BP and hemoglobin
Chest pain returns 8 hours later with new ST elevation
items.rationale: The book lists the evidence of reperfusion after PCI as ST segment resolution, chest pain relief and a sudden rise in CK-MB/troponin (washout from the reopened artery). It also lists reperfusion arrhythmias, but any ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation is still treated and reported, not simply accepted. The high-alert PCI complications are retroperitoneal bleeding (back or flank pain, hypotension, falling hemoglobin) and stent thrombosis (recurrent chest pain with new ischemic ECG changes).

title: Cardiac Tamponade after CABG
sub: 6 hours after coronary bypass surgery · Cardiovascular ICU
profile: 66-year-old woman, 6 hours after coronary artery bypass grafting × 3. Took aspirin until the day of surgery and received heparin during the operation. Mediastinal chest tubes in place.

Notes: Nurses' notes 21:00

Client restless and anxious, keeps asking "what's happening?" Neck veins distended with the head of the bed at 30°. Heart sounds muffled and distant. Skin cool and clammy. Systolic pressure drops 16 mm Hg during inspiration. Mediastinal chest tube output fell from 150 mL/h to 10 mL/h over the last hour; clots seen in the tubing. Sternal incision dressing dry. Incisional pain 4/10.
Nurses' notes 19:00
Awake, following commands, extubated at 18:30. Heart sounds clear. Neck veins flat at 30°. Mediastinal chest tube draining bloody fluid.
Vitals: BP 82/68 mm Hg · HR 128 (sinus tachycardia) · RR 26 · SpO₂ 91% on 4 L nasal cannula · CVP 18 mm Hg · Urine output 15 mL/h · T 37.4 °C (99.3 °F)
BP 118/70 · HR 92 · RR 18 · SpO₂ 97% on 4 L · CVP 8 mm Hg · Urine output 60 mL/h
Labs: Hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL (10.8 at 18:00) · Platelets 112,000/mm³ · K⁺ 4.2 mEq/L · Glucose 164 mg/dL
ECG: sinus tachycardia with electrical alternans. Portable chest x-ray: widened mediastinum.
Orders: Continuous ECG, arterial line and SpO₂ monitoring · Chest tube to suction; record output hourly · Notify surgeon for SBP < 90 mm Hg or chest tube output > 100 mL/h · Dopamine infusion per protocol for hypotension, with IV fluids as prescribed · Analgesic as prescribed

items.stem: Which findings in the client's record from 20:30 to 21:00 are signs of cardiac tamponade? Select all that apply.
options: Neck veins distended, CVP 18 mm Hg
Systolic pressure falls 16 mm Hg on inspiration
items.rationale: The book's signs of tamponade are Beck's triad (raised CVP with JVD, muffled heart sounds, hypotension), a narrow pulse pressure (here 82 − 68 = 14), pulsus paradoxus (a drop of more than 10 mm Hg in BP during inspiration), tachycardia, electrical alternans and a widened mediastinum on chest x-ray. Moderate incisional pain is expected after sternotomy, and a mildly raised glucose is a common stress response after surgery.

items.stem: What is causing the client's hypotension and rising CVP?
options: Blood collecting in the pericardial sac is compressing the heart so it cannot fill and pump
Blood loss through the chest tube has left her hypovolemic
The left ventricle is failing and backing fluid into the lungs
The new grafts have closed, causing a large anterior MI
items.rationale: Tamponade is the rapid build-up of fluid or blood (as little as 200 mL) in the pericardial sac, which compresses the heart and reduces its ability to fill and pump. Surgery and anticoagulation are listed causes. Simple hypovolemia would make the neck veins flat and the CVP low, not high. Left-sided failure would cause crackles and would not muffle the heart sounds, and nothing in the record points to new ischemic ECG changes.

items.stem: Which problem is the nurse's highest priority?
options: Poor tissue perfusion from compression of the heart
Risk for infection of the sternal wound
items.rationale: The book calls tamponade a medical emergency: the compressed heart cannot pump enough blood, causing poor oxygen delivery and tissue perfusion. Her restlessness, cool clammy skin and urine output of 15 mL/h show this is already happening. Pain, infection risk and anxiety matter but are not immediately life-threatening, and her anxiety is itself a sign of poor perfusion.

items.stem: For each intervention, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated for this client now.
rows: Prepare for pericardiocentesis or a return to the OR
Bring the crash cart and defibrillator to the bedside
Give oxygen and be ready for intubation if needed
Start the dopamine infusion with IV fluids as prescribed
Give IV furosemide to bring down the CVP
Recheck vital signs in 1 hour before calling the surgeon
items.rationale: The book's tamponade priorities are to call for help, give oxygen and prepare for intubation if needed, monitor closely, prepare for pericardiocentesis or the OR, and keep the crash cart and defibrillator at the bedside. Dopamine is used together with fluid resuscitation to support blood pressure. The high CVP comes from the squeezed heart, not from too much fluid, so a diuretic would lower filling even further. Waiting an hour delays treatment of a true emergency.

items.stem: Put the nurse's actions in priority order. Tap each in sequence; tap again to undo.
steps: Call for help: notify the surgeon and rapid response team
Increase oxygen and prepare for intubation if needed
Stay with the client and monitor vital signs, mental status, ECG and SpO₂ while the team arrives
Prepare the client for pericardiocentesis or return to the OR once the surgeon decides
items.rationale: The book's nursing priorities for tamponade start with calling for help, because it is a true emergency that only a provider can relieve. Oxygen and airway support come next. While the team is on the way the nurse stays at the bedside and tracks her response, and once the surgeon decides on the procedure the nurse prepares her for pericardiocentesis or, as is usual after cardiac surgery with clotted chest tubes, a return to the OR to remove the blood and free the heart.

items.stem: After the client returns from the OR, where clot was removed from the pericardium: for each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or needs follow-up.
rows: Heart sounds clear and easy to hear
Systolic pressure varies less than 5 mm Hg with breathing
Two hours later: neck veins distended again, BP 90/76 mm Hg
items.rationale: A wider pulse pressure, normal blood pressure, clear heart sounds, the loss of pulsus paradoxus and better urine output show the heart can fill and pump again. Returning JVD with a falling, narrowing blood pressure are the signs of tamponade from the book coming back, so the nurse calls for help again right away.

title: Acute Pancreatitis
sub: Abdominal pain after heavy drinking · Medical-surgical unit
profile: 44-year-old man, 80 kg, admitted from the emergency department with severe abdominal pain that began the day after a weekend of heavy drinking. Drinks 6–8 beers most days.

Notes: Nurses' notes 08:00

Severe, knifelike pain in the mid-epigastric area that goes through to his back, 9/10. Has vomited four times since midnight. Lying curled on his side. Abdomen distended, tender and guarded. Bowel sounds decreased. Bluish bruising on both flanks. Anxious and asking whether he is "going to die." Oriented × 3.
Admission history
Alcohol use as above; no known gallstones. Father had "pancreas problems." Takes ibuprofen as needed for back pain.
Vitals: BP 96/60 mm Hg · HR 122 · RR 26, shallow · SpO₂ 94% on room air · T 38.3 °C (100.9 °F) · Urine output 30 mL/h for the last 2 hours
Labs: Lipase 1,850 units/L · Amylase 940 units/L · Calcium 7.4 mg/dL · Glucose 212 mg/dL · K⁺ 3.2 mEq/L · Mg²⁺ 1.4 mg/dL · Hemoglobin 15.8 g/dL
Abdominal ultrasound: no gallstones. CT abdomen: enlarged, inflamed pancreas with peripancreatic fluid; no necrosis.
Orders: NPO · Lactated Ringer's IV as prescribed · Strict intake and output; urine output hourly · Blood glucose every 6 hours; insulin per protocol · Replace calcium, magnesium and potassium per protocol · Fentanyl IV as prescribed for pain · NG tube to intermittent suction if vomiting continues · Oxygen to keep SpO₂ ≥ 92%

items.stem: Tap the findings in the client's record that are consistent with acute pancreatitis.
passage: Pain goes through to his back
Takes ibuprofen as needed for back pain
items.rationale: The book describes pancreatitis pain as severe, knifelike and deep mid-epigastric, often radiating to the back and starting 12–48 hours after heavy alcohol intake, with nausea and vomiting in up to 90% of cases. Abdominal distention, tenderness and guarding, and decreased bowel sounds are listed exam findings, and flank bruising (Grey Turner sign) is a listed skin sign. Being oriented does not point to the diagnosis, and ibuprofen use is medication history the nurse records, not a finding of pancreatitis.

items.stem: Complete the sentences about the client's lab results.

blanks.pre: The lipase of 1,850 units/L is important because lipase is
opts: more specific to the pancreas than amylase
blanks.answer: more specific to the pancreas than amylase

blanks.pre: The calcium of 7.4 mg/dL is low because
and the glucose of 212 mg/dL is high because
opts: injured beta cells release less insulin
he ate a large meal before admission
blanks.answer: injured beta cells release less insulin

items.rationale: Per the book's diagnostic table, lipase above 60 units/L is more specific to the pancreas than amylase. In pancreatitis, fat necrosis binds free calcium and causes hypocalcemia (below 8.2 mg/dL), and injury to the pancreatic beta cells impairs insulin release and causes hyperglycemia (above 100 mg/dL). He is NPO and receiving lactated Ringer's, which contains no dextrose.

items.stem: Which complication is the client at greatest immediate risk of developing?
items.rationale: BP 96/60, HR 122 and urine output of 30 mL/h in an 80 kg client (below the book's 1 mL/kg/h threshold for hypoperfusion) show he is losing circulating volume. The book's initial management uses IV fluid resuscitation to restore blood volume and prevent hypovolemic shock. Diabetes and pseudocysts are later complications, mainly of chronic pancreatitis, and malnutrition develops over days.

items.stem: Which interventions should the nurse expect to be part of this client's initial plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Give lactated Ringer's IV as prescribed
Replace calcium, magnesium and potassium as prescribed
Offer a high-calorie, high-fat meal to rebuild his strength
items.rationale: The book's initial medical management is NPO to suppress pancreatic enzyme secretion, IV fluid resuscitation such as lactated Ringer's, calcium, magnesium and potassium replacement, and blood glucose checks every 6 hours with insulin if needed. Antibiotics are for infected necrosis or a biliary cause and are not used prophylactically; his CT shows no necrosis and his ultrasound shows no gallstones. Once stable, the diet advances gradually to high-calorie, low-fat meals, never high-fat.

items.stem: Despite being NPO, the client keeps vomiting and his abdomen is more distended. Which prescribed intervention should the nurse carry out now?
options: Insert the NG tube and connect it to intermittent suction
Give clear liquids in small sips to settle his stomach
Place the client flat on his back to relax the abdomen
Hold the IV fluids until the vomiting stops
items.rationale: The book lists an NG tube with intermittent suction to reduce pancreatic stimulation as part of GI support. Oral fluids would stimulate the pancreas, which is why he is NPO. Lying flat does not treat the cause and may worsen comfort and breathing. Holding IV fluids would deepen his hypovolemia.

items.stem: Forty-eight hours later: for each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement, no change, or decline.
items.rationale: Urine output above 1 mL/kg/h (80 mL/h for him), a normal blood pressure and controlled pain show that fluid resuscitation and opioid pain control are working. A rising glucose needs follow-up, since the book notes insulin may be needed. Ongoing distention and nausea mean the abdomen has not settled yet, so he stays NPO with the NG tube to intermittent suction and the diet is not advanced.

title: Cirrhosis with Ascites and Suspected Varices
sub: Increasing abdominal girth and confusion · Medical unit
profile: 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and chronic hepatitis C, admitted for a tense, enlarging abdomen and new forgetfulness. Last drink 3 days ago.

Notes: Nurses' notes 09:00

Abdomen tense and distended with an everted umbilicus and visible veins around the navel (caput medusae). Shifting dullness on percussion. Short of breath when lying flat. Yellow sclera and skin. Spider angiomas on the chest, reddened palms. Gums bleed easily; bruises on both arms. Flapping tremor of the hands when the arms are held out. Forgetful, cannot recall his breakfast, and is irritable. Bowel sounds normal. Abdominal girth 112 cm.
Admission history
Anorexia and nausea for 2 months with muscle wasting in the arms and shoulders, even though his weight has gone up as his abdomen enlarged. Never vaccinated against hepatitis A.
Vitals: BP 112/68 mm Hg · HR 96 · RR 24 · SpO₂ 94% on room air · T 37.0 °C (98.6 °F) · Weight 88 kg (82 kg one month ago)
Labs: AST and ALT elevated · Total bilirubin 4.8 mg/dL · LDH elevated · Albumin 2.4 g/dL · Platelets 78,000/mm³ · INR 1.9 · Na⁺ 132 mEq/L · K⁺ 3.6 mEq/L
Abdominal ultrasound: large-volume ascites; small, nodular liver.
Orders: Diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis today · EGD tomorrow to evaluate for esophageal varices · Daily weight and abdominal girth · Strict intake and output · Vitamin K as prescribed · Lactulose as prescribed · Dietitian consult · Hepatitis A vaccine · Alcohol cessation counseling

items.stem: Which findings indicate complications of the client's cirrhosis that need follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Shifting dullness and an everted umbilicus
Gums bleed easily and bruises on both arms
items.rationale: The book's cirrhosis assessment includes asterixis (flapping tremor), a sign of hepatic encephalopathy, along with neuro changes such as forgetfulness, agitation and disorientation. Shifting dullness and an everted umbilicus point to ascites, and easy bruising and bleeding gums are bleeding signs. Normal bowel sounds and a normal temperature do not need follow-up.

items.stem: Complete the sentence.

blanks.pre: Scar tissue in the liver obstructs blood flow, causing
which leads to complications such as
and fluid retention is made worse by

items.rationale: The book explains that cirrhotic scarring obstructs blood flow through the liver, causing portal hypertension and complications such as ascites, esophageal varices and hepatorenal syndrome. In alcohol-related cirrhosis, fluid retention also comes from decreased albumin and hormonal changes. His albumin of 2.4 g/dL fits. His platelets are low and his bilirubin is high, not the reverse.

items.stem: A large volume of fluid is planned for removal during today's paracentesis. Which complication is the nurse most concerned about?
items.rationale: The book warns that rapid removal of fluid from the abdomen lowers abdominal pressure, causing vasodilation and hypovolemic shock. Fluid overload is the problem paracentesis treats, not a risk of it. Hepatitis A is a vaccination concern, not a procedure risk. Loss of the gag reflex is a concern after EGD, not paracentesis.

items.stem: For each intervention, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated in the client's plan of care.
rows: Measure abdominal girth and monitor fluids and electrolytes
Keep the client on strict bed rest
items.rationale: The book's core interventions are monitoring fluids, electrolytes, medicines and abdominal girth, nutrition management, and teaching alcohol cessation. Medical treatment includes vitamin K and blood products, and the hepatitis A vaccine is recommended in chronic liver disease. The book says to encourage mobility, so strict bed rest is not part of the plan.

items.stem: Before the EGD, a new prescription arrives to insert a nasogastric tube for nausea. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Hold the insertion and contact the provider about the risk of rupturing varices
Insert the NG tube using extra lubricant to protect the esophagus
Insert the NG tube after giving vitamin K
Ask another nurse to insert the tube
items.rationale: The book warns that when esophageal varices are suspected an NG tube should not be inserted, because of the risk of variceal rupture and massive hemorrhage. Current guidance treats this as a strong caution rather than an absolute ban, but here the varices have not yet been evaluated, his INR is 1.9 and his platelets are 78,000/mm³, and the tube is only for nausea, so the nurse holds the insertion and clarifies the order with the provider. Extra lubricant, vitamin K or a different nurse does not remove that risk.

items.stem: After the paracentesis and, the next day, the EGD: for each finding, indicate whether it is an expected outcome or needs follow-up.
rows: Abdominal girth down to 101 cm and breathing easier
Thirty minutes after paracentesis: BP 82/50 mm Hg, HR 124, dizzy
Shortly after the EGD the client asks for water; gag reflex not yet returned
items.rationale: Less abdominal girth, less weight and easier breathing show that fluid was removed as planned. Hypotension with tachycardia and dizziness after paracentesis is the hypovolemic shock the book warns about and must be reported at once. After an EGD the nurse waits for the gag reflex to return before giving anything by mouth, so the request for water must be held.
